title: Basic Concepts And Models
notes: Open by making the central contrast vivid: on a line a distribution can be scanned from left to right, while on a circle the zero direction is a coordinate convention. This lecture builds the three reusable views of a circular law: arc probabilities, integer moments, and named model generators.

title: Three Views Of One Circular Law
notes: Use the triangle as the organizing picture for the chapter. The distribution function answers probability questions about arcs, the characteristic sequence stores the Fourier coordinates, and the model family supplies a generative story. A good circular analysis should let students move among all three.

title: Circular Distribution Functions Need A Cut
notes: Emphasize that the cut is useful but not intrinsic. Once a zero direction and orientation are chosen, the unwrapped distribution function increases by one after a full turn. The probability object is the arc mass; the plotted function is a coordinate device for computing it.

title: Arc Probabilities Survive The Cut
notes: This is the practical repair for the discontinuity at the cut point. If the target arc does not cross zero, take an ordinary difference of F values. If it does cross zero, split it into two ordinary intervals and add the masses. The notebook check records the two computations agreeing to about six times ten to the minus four on the plotting grid.

title: Characteristic Functions Become Sequences
notes: Explain why the allowed frequencies are integers. The angle theta and theta plus 2pi represent the same point, so exp(i p theta) is single valued on the circle only when p is an integer. The real and imaginary parts are the cosine and sine trigonometric moments.

title: Fourier Reconstruction Reads The Density Back
notes: Connect the characteristic sequence to an inspectable density. Low harmonics recover broad features such as mean direction and axiality; higher harmonics sharpen local peaks. The point is not to memorize a formula but to see moments as coordinates for circular shape.

title: Uniform Is The Reference Law
notes: Use uniformity as the zero signal in the Fourier picture. The density is constant, every nonzero integer coefficient vanishes, and arc probability is exactly proportional to arc length. This gives the baseline for later tests of concentration or multimodality.

title: Von Mises: Exponential Tilt Around A Direction
notes: Present von Mises as the likelihood-friendly circular analogue of a normal peak. The parameter mu selects the modal direction and kappa controls concentration. The notebook matches a target resultant length rho by solving the Bessel ratio A(kappa) equals I1(kappa) over I0(kappa).

title: Cardioid: A First Harmonic Perturbation
notes: The cardioid family is useful because it is transparent in the Fourier basis. It adds only a first harmonic to the uniform law, so it can model mild unimodal departure from uniformity without introducing a long tail of coefficients.

title: Wrapped Families Fold A Line Onto A Circle
notes: A wrapped model begins with a real-valued variable and reduces it modulo one revolution. The density is a sum over all integer shifts, while the characteristic coefficients have simple damping patterns. Wrapped normal coefficients decay like rho to p squared; wrapped Cauchy coefficients decay like rho to the absolute value of p.

title: Projection Models Discard Radius
notes: Projection is a different generative story from wrapping. Start with a planar vector, keep only its angle, and the radial information disappears. Anisotropic planar variation can create strong axial structure even when the projected angular mean is near zero.

title: Model Fingerprints In Low Moments
notes: Use this slide to compare families without pretending that two moments identify every distribution. The first two amplitudes already separate several stories: cardioid stops after the first harmonic, von Mises carries a smaller second harmonic, wrapped Cauchy decays geometrically, and the zero-mean projected normal is mostly axial.

title: Convolution Is Multiplication Of Moments
notes: This is the circular version of a familiar characteristic-function rule. If independent angles are added modulo one turn, their integer coefficients multiply. The notebook's wrapped-normal check verifies that the density convolution and the coefficient product agree to numerical precision.

title: Choosing A Model Family
notes: Frame model choice as matching the scientific mechanism rather than choosing the prettiest curve. Uniform means no preferred direction, von Mises means a single concentrated mode, cardioid means a mild first harmonic departure, wrapped models come from linear noise, and projected models come from planar vectors.

title: Notebook Diagnostics As Evidence
notes: Point out that the chapter notebook is not just drawing pictures. It checks normalization, arc split consistency, moment identities, Bessel-ratio matching, projection integrity, and convolution. These diagnostics make the lecture claims reproducible rather than purely visual.

title: Operational Checklist
notes: Close with a procedure students can reuse. First state the probability question as an oriented arc. Second choose whether a distribution function, moment sequence, or generator is the cleanest representation. Third inspect the first coefficients, reconstruct if needed, and then test the model family by the invariant it promises.
